ana_01.label: Dataset shape and coverage
ana_01.content: The dataset covers 2,266 seasons of 868 distinct TV dramas (876 distinct IMDb title IDs — a few titles share names) airing between January 1990 and October 2018. Every column is fully populated: there are zero missing values for titleId, seasonNumber, title, date, av_rating, share, or genres. The sole numeric outcome is av_rating (the IMDb-weighted season average) which ranges from 2.704 to 9.682 with a mean of 8.06 and a median of 8.12. Already from this profile we see TV-drama ratings on IMDb skew strongly upward — this is normal for IMDb, which is a self-selected audience that mostly votes on shows it likes.

ana_02.label: Distribution of IMDb season ratings
ana_02.content: The full distribution of season-level IMDb scores is heavily right-skewed toward 7.5–8.5. Out of 2,266 seasons, 1,391 (61%) fall in the [7.5, 8.5) range. Only 93 seasons (4.1%) crack the 9.0 threshold, and just 4 seasons (0.18%) reach 9.5+. The bottom of the distribution is thin — fewer than 30 seasons sit below 6.5, and the absolute floor is a single Reality-TV-tagged season at 2.70. This shape — a tall hump at 8.0 with a long thin upper tail — is what makes a 'prestige tier' visible at all.

data_table.description: Histogram of season IMDb ratings, 0.5-wide bins

ana_03.label: Yearly mean rating drifts upward
ana_03.content: Mean season rating per year drifts upward over the 29-year span: the 1990–1999 decade averages 7.83, the 2000s 8.02, and the 2010–2018 stretch 8.11 — a gain of about 0.28 of a rating point from the first decade to the last. The rise is not monotonic; the late 1990s actually look slightly worse than 1990 itself, with a low of 7.63 in 1996. The break-point is 2001, when the mean jumps to 8.06 and never falls back below 8.0 again (with the mild exception of 2007). This 0.28-point gap is small relative to the within-year noise (std of mean is roughly 0.05) but it is consistent across two-thirds of the series and therefore meaningful.

data_table.description: Year-by-year season count and mean / median rating, 1990-2018

ana_04.label: Prestige-tier (>=9.0) seasons per year
ana_04.content: If you isolate the prestige tier — seasons rated 9.0 or higher — the picture is much sharper than the headline mean suggests. Throughout the 2000s there are essentially zero such seasons most years (1999, 2000, 2001, 2002, 2003 each have one or none). Then in 2014 the count jumps to 13, followed by 14 in 2015, 12 in 2016, and a dataset peak of 16 in 2017. By percentage of seasons that year, 1992 and 1996 had 0% above 9.0, while 2014 had 7.83% and 2017 had 6.96%. So while the mean rating drift from the 1990s to the 2010s is modest, the rate at which prestige-tier seasons are produced rose roughly tenfold.

data_table.description: Number of seasons rated >=9.0 per year, with total seasons and percentage

ana_05.label: Volume of TV drama seasons grew 7-fold
ana_05.content: The number of drama seasons listed on IMDb explodes across the period: 22 in 1990, 32 in 2000, 98 in 2010, peaking at 230 in 2017 before tapering to 184 in 2018 (likely truncated by an October data cutoff). The 2010–2018 window contains 1,468 seasons, more than seven times the 207 seasons in the entire 1990–1999 decade. This is the dataset's reflection of the 'Peak TV' phenomenon FX's John Landgraf named in 2015 — and it is essential context for the rating trend, because a denser top tier emerges naturally when more shows are being made.

ana_06.label: Top 20 highest-rated seasons in the dataset
ana_06.content: The single highest-rated season in the dataset is improbably Parenthood season 1 (1990) at 9.68, but with a vote share of just 1.68% — a thin sample. The top of the list is dominated by recent prestige cable: Breaking Bad season 5 (2013, 9.55, 18.95% share), Game of Thrones season 6 (2016, 9.49) and 4 (2014, 9.43), BoJack Horseman season 5 (2018, 9.47), True Detective season 1 (2014, 9.33), Sherlock season 2 (2012, 9.32). Several early entries (Touched by an Angel season 5, Are You Afraid of the Dark? season 3) hold high ratings but on tiny vote shares (<3%), reflecting a survivorship-and-fan-loyalty effect rather than mass acclaim. The high-share, high-rating cluster — Breaking Bad, Game of Thrones, Sherlock, Suits — is unambiguously a 2010s phenomenon.

ana_07.label: Within-show arc of landmark prestige series
ana_07.content: Several flagship 2000s/2010s dramas show clear within-show rating arcs that bend upward toward the finale: Breaking Bad climbs 8.71 → 9.55 across five seasons; Mad Men 8.23 → 8.81; Game of Thrones starts at 9.13 and peaks at 9.49 in season 6 before pulling back to 9.30 in season 7. The Sopranos is remarkably stable at 8.40–8.88. The Wire holds tight in the 8.24–8.42 band through all five seasons. Six Feet Under has a celebrated finale season at 8.93. Compare True Detective, which crashes from 9.33 (season 1) to 8.19 (season 2). These arcs are central to what readers mean when they say a show 'stuck the landing' — and only Breaking Bad and Game of Thrones manage a strict monotonic ascent across the dataset.

data_table.description: Season-by-season ratings for landmark prestige dramas

ana_08.label: Genre-level rating gain from 1990s to 2010s
ana_08.content: Decomposing the rating drift by genre (only those with ≥30 total seasons): History rises a striking +1.49 (from 6.79 in the 1990s, n=1, to 8.28 in the 2010s, n=54), Horror +0.69, Adventure +0.66, Action +0.43, Comedy +0.34, Drama +0.28. Two genres actually fell: Sci-Fi (-0.16) and Thriller (-0.29). The rise is therefore broad — most of the genres that supply the top of the IMDb scoreboard improved — but unevenly distributed. Crime drama, the genre most associated culturally with prestige TV (Sopranos, The Wire, Breaking Bad), gained a moderate +0.22 from 7.92 to 8.15.

ana_09.label: Within-show season-arc curve (across 293 multi-season shows)
ana_09.content: Pooling all shows with at least three seasons in the dataset (n=293), mean rating actually rises through the early seasons and peaks at season 5 (mean 8.32, n=154), then falls steadily through season 12 (7.91, n=12). On a per-show basis, the average finale rating is +0.08 above the average premiere rating — and 58% of shows ended on a higher note than they started. So the cliché 'shows decline after season 4' is partly false: at the population level, prestige drama improves into season 5 before fatigue sets in.

data_table.description: Mean season rating by season number, across all shows with >=3 seasons

ana_10.label: Top 10 risers and fallers (last season minus first season)
ana_10.content: Ranking shows by how much their final season's rating exceeded their first, the biggest 'late-bloomers' include Criminal Minds (+1.85 across 14 seasons), Friday Night Lights (+1.72), BoJack Horseman (+1.69), and Homicide: Life on the Street (+1.29). At the other end, the steepest 'falls from grace' are Are You Afraid of the Dark? (-2.34), Lethal Weapon (-2.31), Dexter (-1.97 — the famous lumberjack-finale collapse), Scrubs (-1.95), The Walking Dead (-1.68), and True Blood (-1.35). These are the shows audiences argue about; they make the trend finding feel real because they isolate concrete reputations.

caveats.content: av_rating is IMDb's weighted average, not a raw mean — the algorithm is undisclosed and recomputed daily, so exact values may differ from a fresh IMDb pull.

Vote shares are wildly unequal: Breaking Bad season 5 has 18.95% of its show's votes, while Touched by an Angel season 5 has 0.08%. Some of the highest-scoring early-1990s entries (Parenthood S1, L.A. Law S4, Santa Barbara S1) are based on tiny samples and likely not representative of broad opinion.
Sample sizes are tiny early in the period (10 seasons in 1992, 17 in 1991) versus 215+ in 2016-2017, so any year-on-year volatility before ~2000 is amplified by small-N noise.
2018 is incomplete (data cutoff October 10, 2018), so its 184-season count is an undercount and shouldn't be compared directly to 2017's 230.

IMDb voters self-select; they are disproportionately young, male, English-speaking, and engaged. The trend is therefore in IMDb-voter-consensus quality, which is correlated with — but not identical to — 'objective' television quality.
